name: Soviet Crewed Lunar Program
short_status: Cancelled May 1974 and kept secret until the late 1980s: the USSR's two-track effort to beat Apollo. Cosmonaut-class Zond hardware looped the Moon uncrewed, but all four launches of the N1 Moon rocket failed and no Soviet ever left Earth orbit.
tagline: Soviet Union · Programme · 1964 · The space race Cancelled
stats: N1 Moon-rocket launches, 1969 to 1972, none successful
NK-15 engines on the N1 first stage
cosmonaut the LK lander would set down (vs Apollo's 2)
cancelled, then kept secret until the late 1980s

facts.label: Program go-ahead
facts.value: 3 Aug 1964 Central Committee/Council of Ministers decree set the goal of a crewed lunar landing, split into the L1 circumlunar effort and the N1-L3 landing effort, both using lunar-orbit rendezvous

facts.label: Two parallel programs
facts.value: L1/Zond: a stripped Soyuz 7K-L1 sent around the Moon on a Proton-K. N1/L3: the giant N1 rocket carrying the LOK orbiter and LK lander for a landing

facts.label: N1 rocket
facts.value: 105.3 m tall, about 2,750 t at liftoff, 30 NK-15 engines on the first stage (Block A) producing roughly 45,780 kN of sea-level thrust; the largest engine cluster ever flown on a first stage

facts.label: L3 landing architecture
facts.value: Two-cosmonaut LOK (Soyuz 7K-LOK) orbiter plus a single-cosmonaut LK lander; the crew member transferred from LOK to LK by an external spacewalk rather than through an internal tunnel

facts.label: LK lander
facts.value: Launch mass about 5,560 to 6,525 kg; the single Blok E engine (about 20 kN) handled both final descent and ascent; roughly 40% the mass of Apollo's Lunar Module

facts.label: Assigned cosmonauts
facts.value: The landing group was led by Alexei Leonov, the strongest candidate to be first Soviet on the Moon, with Oleg Makarov as LOK pilot; backup pairs included Valeri Bykovsky and Pavel Popovich

facts.label: N1 flight 3L
facts.value: 21 Feb 1969, Baikonur Site 110; the KORD control system shut the engines down about 68 seconds after liftoff after a fire in the tail; the rocket was destroyed

facts.label: N1 flight 5L (pad disaster)
facts.value: 3 Jul 1969; a first-stage engine exploded at liftoff, the rocket rose about 200 m, fell back onto Launch Complex 110 and detonated, leveling the pad in one of the largest artificial non-nuclear explosions on record; rebuilding took roughly 18 months

facts.label: N1 flights 6L and 7L
facts.value: 6L (27 Jun 1971, 23:15 UTC Jun 26) lost roll control and broke up near 50 seconds; 7L (23 Nov 1972) flew farthest but a propellant line burst near first-stage shutdown at about 107 seconds

facts.label: LK uncrewed Earth-orbit tests
facts.value: Three T2K articles flew successfully under Cosmos cover names: Cosmos 379 (24 Nov 1970), Cosmos 398 (26 Feb 1971) and Cosmos 434 (12 Aug 1971); the LK was judged ready for a crewed flight

facts.label: Cosmos 434 Australian scare
facts.value: When the last LK test article reentered over Australia on 22 Aug 1981, the Soviet Foreign Ministry publicly admitted it was an 'experimental unit of a lunar cabin' and carried no nuclear material

facts.label: Cancellation
facts.value: In May 1974 chief designer Vasily Mishin was fired and replaced by Valentin Glushko, who halted the N1 and the crewed lunar landing; the N1 was formally closed out in 1976, the program never publicly admitted until glasnost

timeline: Decree formally sets the crewed lunar goal, splitting it into the L1 circumlunar and N1-L3 landing programs
Zond 4, an uncrewed L1 circumlunar test, flies away from the Moon; its self-destruct fires on a failed reentry over the Gulf of Guinea
Zond 5 loops the Moon and returns with two tortoises: the first circumlunar flight-and-return by any nation
/moon/missions/zond-5
Zond 6 circles the Moon but a gasket leak depressurizes the cabin, killing the biological payload; the parachute cuts early and the capsule crashes in Kazakhstan, though its film is recovered
First N1 launch (3L) from Baikonur; a tail fire triggers engine shutdown at about 68 seconds and the rocket is lost
Second N1 (5L) falls back onto Launch Complex 110 seconds after liftoff and detonates, wrecking the pad in one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded
Zond 7 flies a fully successful circumlunar mission with color photography, the only L1 flight that would have been safe for a crew, weeks after Apollo 11 had already landed
Zond 8 completes another successful circumlunar flight and Indian Ocean recovery
Cosmos 379, the first uncrewed LK lander test, flies in Earth orbit under a cover name
Cosmos 398, the second LK Earth-orbit test, succeeds
Third N1 (6L, 23:15 UTC on Jun 26) loses roll control and breaks up around 50 seconds
Cosmos 434, the third and last LK test, flies successfully; the lander is declared ready for crew
Fourth N1 (7L) flies farthest but a propellant line bursts near staging at about 107 seconds; it is the last N1 ever launched
May 1974
Mishin is fired and Glushko cancels the N1 and the crewed lunar landing; two nearly complete rockets are scrapped
The Cosmos 434 LK test article reenters over Australia; Moscow admits it was a 'lunar cabin' and carried no nuclear material
Under glasnost the USSR finally acknowledges the N1-L3 program and publishes its history
